## Important comparability caveats before the answer

**1. The excerpts do not contain capacity (ASM) data.** The industry-standard efficiency metrics — CASM and CASM‑ex‑fuel — cannot be computed. The corpus contains only revenue, fuel expense, salaries/benefits, and operating income [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt, "Selected figures from each company's fiscal year 2024 Form 10-K... Total operating revenue / Aircraft fuel expense / Salaries, wages and benefits / Operating income"]. I therefore use **cost-to-revenue ratios**, which are a proxy for *profitability*, not pure unit cost — a carrier with strong pricing power (premium cabin, loyalty, long-haul) will look "efficient" even with a high CASM.

**2. Alaska is not comparable to its own history or to the others on a like-for-like basis** — Alaska Air Group's FY2024 consolidates Hawaiian Airlines only from the September 2024 close, so its figures are a partial-year blend of two cost structures.

**3. Southwest's network is structurally different** — short-haul, point-to-point, single-fleet. Low stage length mechanically inflates unit cost, so raw CASM comparisons against Delta/United long-haul networks are not apples-to-apples in either direction.

**4. Fiscal years do align** — all five are calendar-year filers (Jan 1 – Dec 31) [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

## Derived FY2024 cost structure (total opex = revenue − operating income)

| Airline | Revenue | Implied Opex | Opex/Rev | Op. Margin | Fuel/Rev | Labor/Rev | Ex-fuel Opex/Rev |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| United | $57,063M | $51,967M | 91.1% | 8.93% | 20.6% | 29.2% | **70.5%** |
| Alaska | $11,735M | $11,165M | 95.1% | 4.86% | 21.4% | 30.6% | 73.8% |
| American | $54,211M | $51,597M | 95.2% | 4.82% | 21.1% | 29.6% | 74.1% |
| Southwest | $27,483M | $27,162M | 98.8% | 1.17% | 21.2% | **44.5%** | 77.7% |

## Interpretation

- **Delta** converts revenue to profit best: it absorbs only 90.3 cents of cost per revenue dollar and has the lowest fuel intensity (17.1% of revenue), reflecting its Trainer refinery and premium/loyalty revenue mix.
- **United** is arguably the leaner operator on a *controllable* basis — lowest ex-fuel opex at 70.5% of revenue — but higher fuel intensity pushes its total ratio above Delta's.
- **Southwest** is the clear outlier: labor alone consumes 44.5% of revenue and total costs consume 98.8%, leaving a 1.17% operating margin.
- **American and Alaska** are nearly identical in the middle (~95% opex/revenue), though Alaska's figure is distorted by the Hawaiian consolidation.

**Bottom line:** Delta on a total cost-to-revenue and margin basis; United if you isolate ex-fuel (controllable) cost. Note this ranks cost *absorption*, not unit cost — a true CASM-ex ranking would likely favor Southwest's low-cost single-fleet model and is not verifiable from these excerpts.

ANSWER: Delta Air Lines — lowest total operating cost as a share of revenue (90.3%) and the highest operating margin (9.73%) of the five in FY2024; United is a close second and actually leads on ex-fuel cost (70.5% of revenue), while Southwest is the least efficient (98.8% opex/revenue, 1.17% margin). Caveat: no ASM data is available in the source, so this is a cost-to-revenue proxy rather than a true CASM/CASM-ex comparison, and Alaska's FY2024 includes a partial year of Hawaiian.
